title: Consecutive symbolic powers at a height-one prime of a Krull domain embed into its prime quotient
statement:
Let $D$ be a commutative integral domain with fraction field $F$. A height-one prime means a nonzero prime ideal having no prime strictly between $(0)$ and it. Suppose (i) for each height-one prime $Q$, the localization $D_Q$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]; (ii) $D=\bigcap_{\mathrm{ht}(Q)=1}D_Q$ inside $F$, with an empty intersection meaning $F$; and (iii) every nonzero element of $D$ belongs to only finitely many height-one primes. Fix a height-one prime $P$. For each integer $n\ge0$, put
$$P^{(n)}=\{a\in D:a/1\in (PD_P)^n\},$$
so $P^{(0)}=D$. Then for every $n\ge0$ there exists an injective $D$-linear map
$$P^{(n)}/P^{(n+1)}\longrightarrow D/P,$$
where the source is the quotient of the indicated $D$-submodules and both modules have their natural scalar actions. No Noetherianity of $D$ or of $D/P$ is assumed.

source.place: Swanson–Huneke, Integral Closure of Ideals, Rings, and Modules, Definition 4.10.1 and Theorem 4.10.7 (Mori–Nishimura), first two proof paragraphs, printed pp.92–93 (PDF pp.105–106, zero-based). Read online at https://www.math.purdue.edu/~iswanso/book/SwansonHuneke.pdf; local PDF WANTED. The injection of consecutive symbolic-power quotients is the intermediate assertion, not the Noetherianity criterion.

proof.text: For every height-one prime $Q$, primes of $D_Q$ correspond, with inclusions and contraction, to primes of $D$ contained in $Q$. These are exactly $(0)$ and $Q$. Thus $D_Q$ has dimension one and maximal ideal $QD_Q$. Hypothesis (i) supplies Noetherianity and normality, so the one-dimensional normal local domain criterion makes $D_Q$ a discrete valuation ring.

Choose a generator $t$ of the nonzero maximal ideal of $D_P$. Write $t=a/u$ with $a\in D$ and $u\in D\setminus P$. Since $u$ is a unit in $D_P$, the nonzero element $a$ also generates $PD_P$. Contraction of $PD_P$ is $P$, so $a\in P$. Fix $n\ge0$ and let $S$ be the finite set of height-one primes $Q\ne P$ containing $a$, finite by (iii).

source.place: Theorem 4.10.7, first two proof paragraphs, printed pp.92–93; online PDF pp.105–106 (zero-based) read. Local PDF WANTED. The worker supplies a denominator-clearing variant avoiding the auxiliary ring D[x].

proof.text: For $Q\in S$, distinct height-one primes are incomparable, so choose $b_Q\in Q\setminus P$. In the DVR $D_Q$, choose a uniformizer $\pi_Q$ and use unit-times-power factorization to write $a=u_Q\pi_Q^{e_Q}$ and $b_Q=w_Q\pi_Q^{f_Q}$. Both exponents are positive: exponent zero would make the element a unit, whereas both lie in $QD_Q$. Put $s=\prod_{Q\in S}b_Q^{ne_Q}$. Then $s\notin P$ by primality. At $Q\in S$, the exponent $ne_Qf_Q\ge ne_Q$ shows $b_Q^{ne_Q}/a^n\in D_Q$; the other factors belong to $D_Q$, so $s/a^n\in D_Q$. At a height-one $Q\notin S\cup\{P\}$, $a$ is a unit in $D_Q$, giving the same inclusion. Empty products equal $1$; this calculation also covers $n=0$.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.7, first two proof paragraphs, printed pp.92–93; online PDF pp.105–106 (zero-based) read. Local PDF WANTED. The worker supplies a denominator-clearing variant avoiding the auxiliary ring D[x].

proof.text: For $x\in P^{(n)}$, the fraction $sx/a^n$ belongs to $D_P$, because $P^{(n)}D_P\subseteq (PD_P)^n=a^nD_P$. At every other height-one prime it belongs to $D_Q$ by the preceding calculation and $x\in D$. Hypothesis (ii) therefore gives $sx/a^n\in D$. Hence $f_n:P^{(n)}\to D/P$, $x\mapsto sx/a^n+P$, is defined. Multiplication by the fixed fraction $s/a^n$ commutes with addition and multiplication by $D$, proving $D$-linearity.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.7, first two proof paragraphs, printed pp.92–93; online PDF pp.105–106 (zero-based) read. Local PDF WANTED. The worker supplies a denominator-clearing variant avoiding the auxiliary ring D[x].

proof.text: Contraction of $PD_P$ is $P$. Since $s$ is a unit in $D_P$, for $x\in P^{(n)}$ the kernel condition is equivalently $sx/a^n\in P$, equivalently $sx/a^n\in PD_P=aD_P$, equivalently $x\in a^{n+1}D_P$. By the definition of symbolic powers the last condition is $x\in P^{(n+1)}$. Thus $\ker f_n=P^{(n+1)}$; no assertion about finite generation of either symbolic power was used.

source.place: Theorem 4.10.7, first two proof paragraphs, printed pp.92–93; online PDF pp.105–106 (zero-based) read. Local PDF WANTED. The worker supplies a denominator-clearing variant avoiding the auxiliary ring D[x].

proof.text: The symbolic powers are $D$-submodules and $P^{(n+1)}\subseteq P^{(n)}$, by taking inverse images of the corresponding nested ideals of $D_P$. Define the required map by $[x]\mapsto f_n(x)$. Changing $x$ by an element of $P^{(n+1)}$ does not change the image, and a class maps to zero precisely when its representative lies in $P^{(n+1)}$, by the kernel calculation. This proves well-definedness and injectivity, and linearity descends from $f_n$.
